articles.title: Pay Per Use: when AI uses your work, you should get paid
articles.text:
Pay Per Use: when AI uses your work, you should get paid
AI answer engines read a publisher’s page and hand the reader a summary, so the visit, and the revenue that would come with it, never happens. Most publishers will never sign a licensing deal with the companies that use their work in AI products, and no company can negotiate with millions of sites. The web needs a way to say “yes, if you pay.” Pay Per Use is one way to say it, and it's now in beta.
In July, we outlined our plan for Pay Per Use. Since then, we’ve been working with buyers and content owners to bring it to life. The gist: A buyer offers a price for a specific use of your content. You choose whether to accept. The buyer reports each use, and Cloudflare bills the buyer and pays you. Publishers track usage and earnings in the Cloudflare dashboard. Buyers report usage through a single API.
Pay for the use, not the crawl
AI products fetch far more than they use. A search engine indexes pages it never shows. Charging for every crawl makes the buyer pay before it knows what it needs, and many buyers won't. Paying for use ties the price to the value the buyer actually gets, which we hope brings more buyers to the table and more money to publishers. Pay Per Crawl, which we launched in 2025, charges for access. Pay Per Use pays for what happens next. Publishers can choose the model that suits them.
For buyers, the case is just as simple. Some of the content your product needs is behind a block or a paywall today, and it’s the content that changes fastest: news, research, specialist trade publications. Pay Per Use lets buyers make an offer. You pay only for the content your product actually uses, you’re identified to every publisher as a verified buyer, and one API connects you to every site that says yes. You won’t need thousands of integrations or individually-negotiated contracts.
Each AI company defines the use it will pay for and sets a price. Publishers decide which offers to accept, and then can see how often their content is used and what it has earned. Cloudflare handles enrollment, usage records, billing, and payment.
How Pay Per Use works
Pay Per Use lets publishers make their content available to identified AI companies on terms that turn downstream use into revenue. Publishers choose which programs to join and retain control over crawler access and downstream uses. AI companies identify their crawling activity using Verified bots and, when permitted by the publisher’s controls, can access and index content owned by the publisher. That content can later power many experiences: a cited answer in AI search, a passage quoted in a research agent's report, a product review weighed by a shopping agent, or a recipe adapted by a cooking assistant.
Let’s show how it works!
1. Define what counts as a paid use
Each AI company sets up its program with Cloudflare. It identifies its crawler, defines the use it will pay for, sets a price, and connects a payment account.
Consider two possible offers. A search service could pay when it returns an excerpt from an enrolled page to a customer. A shopping agent could pay when an enrolled review shapes a recommendation. Under the second offer, payment follows use even if the shopper never reads the review.
The same article can create value in different products and publishers can accept different payment offers for different uses. The buyer proposes the definition of the use being paid for; Cloudflare provides the reporting and payment infrastructure.
2. Publishers choose whether to participate
Publishers review offers in the Cloudflare dashboard, under Monetize → Pay Per Use: it will show the AI company, the use it pays for, and its offer price. Publishers decide whether to accept, and can stop participating if an arrangement no longer works for them. There is no origin change or technical integration with each AI company. Each program’s terms also define what the AI company may do with the content, including any restrictions on training.
3. The buyer reports each use
The buyer fetches the list of domains that have accepted its offer, then reports each use as one line of JSON: when it happened, the URL the content came from, and an event ID.
curl -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/$ACCOUNT_ID/pay-per-use/usage-reports" \
 -H "Authorization: Bearer $API_TOKEN" \
 -H "Content-Type: application/jsonl" \
 --data-binary @- <<'EOF'
{"used_at":"2026-09-15T13:42:04Z","url":"https://example.com/article/1","id":"request-001"}
EOF
Usage is self-reported: the program terms require complete reporting, and Cloudflare checks that each reported use maps to an enrolled publisher.
4. Cloudflare settles both sides
We aggregate reported uses, charge the buyer, and pay publishers monthly through their connected payment account. Buyers get one integration. Publishers get one place to see offers and earnings.
Payment is only half the product
Today, publishers see how often each AI company uses their content and what it has earned, by domain and over time. Business Insights already shows which crawlers visit and what they take. Pay Per Use shows what happens next: whether that content was actually used, how often, and what it earned.
Next, we’re working with AI companies to report to publishers more context about each use, such as the keywords that led to the citation, the topic of the request, or the product it powered, with no personal data being exchanged.
Our Answer Engine Optimization (AEO) tool shows how assistants answer questions about your work. Pay Per Use shows what buyers report using, and what that use earned. Together, they connect how your content is found, how it's used, and what it pays.
That helps with two kinds of decisions. Commercial ones: which content earns, which uses are worth it, and whether to keep participating. And editorial ones: what to cover, what to update, and what to make easier for agents to find.
What comes next
During the beta, we’re working directly with each buyer and with the publishers who opt in. The question is simple: do both sides want to keep going? Buyers need content that improves their products at a price that works. Publishers need a return that makes participation worthwhile, reporting they can trust, and payments that arrive on time.
Over time, we want new buyers to onboard with their own products and payment models, without rebuilding enrollment, reporting, and settlement for each publisher.
For publishers, that means one place to accept or decline offers, counter on price, and price content differently by use. Last week’s reporting may be worth more to an AI product than a ten-year-old archive page, and you should be able to charge for that.
The beta will help us determine how to make those choices simple and practical at scale.
Building an economic layer for the agentic web
Content should be able to reach new audiences and generate sustainable revenue, even when it becomes part of someone else's product: a cited search result, a shopping recommendation, an agent's report. Pay Per Use turns those uses into a commercial relationship. A buyer makes an offer, a publisher chooses whether to accept, and the use of valuable content leads to payments and records of what happened.
Not everything should be sold the same way. High-value content needs a trusted network of verified buyers who report how they use it, and that's Pay Per Use. APIs, tools, and data are frequently different, because every request is the use. For those, Monetization Gateway (also in beta as of today) lets sellers charge agents per request, using the open x402 protocol. The two run on the same foundations: identity, metering, pricing, and analytics.
Publishers shouldn't have to choose between blocking every agent and giving their work away. Pay Per Use gives them a way to say yes, on clear terms, with an account of what happened.

articles.title: Snapmaker launches its U1 3D printer that will appeal to creators, hobbyists and newcomers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Leading technology company Snapmaker has launched its new U1 3D printer in Australia which is aimed at a broader range of customers, including creators, educators, hobbyists, and small businesses.
The Snapmaker U1 is a 4-toolhead 3D printer and can make multi-colour and multi-material 3D prints faster and more efficiently.
The printer was first launched through Kickstarter last year where it received support from 20,680 backers and raised $US20.6 million.
The attraction of the new unit is its ease of use which will make it easier for newcomers to 3D printing to get started.
Conventional multi-colour systems load different filaments through the same nozzle but the U1 has four independent tool heads, with each colour or material loaded on its own filament path.
So when a print requires a different colour or material, the unit swaps the entire tool head instead of unloading and reloading filament through the same nozzle.
Snapmaker says a typical tool change takes about 5 seconds.
Another benefit of its tool changer architecture is the substantial reduction in waste associated with multi-colour printing.
Snapmaker says the U1 produce up to 85 per cent less filament waste than shared-nozzle filament-switching 3D printers.
Apart from different coloured filament, the Snapmaker U1 also allows users to use different types of filament for their prints.
New types of filament include rigid and flexible filaments or dedicated support materials so you can produce more complex functional parts while reducing the need for manual material changes.
The UI can automatically calibrate the multiple toolheads, load filament, and monitor the print.
There is even a small camera built in so users can connect via the companion app to see the progress of their work.
The Snapmaker U1 has a build volume at 270 x 270 x 270 mm which is a generous amount of space for your 3D prints.
“Making digital creation more accessible has always been central to Snapmaker,” says Sheila She, Head of Global Go-to-Market at Snapmaker.
“We designed the U1 to make multi-colour and multi-material printing faster, cleaner, and easier to use, while reducing the material waste commonly associated with filament changes.
“We’re excited for Australian customers to discover and experience tool changing 3D printing.”
The Snapmaker U1 is available now for pre-order through JB Hi-Fi and Harvey Norman at the discounted price of $1,299.
The Snapmaker U1 will go on sale on October 15 and will be priced at $1,399.

articles.title: Australians falling victim to a new scam and calling cybercriminals - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Australians have been advised over the years to not click on suspicious links or answer unknown numbers but cybercriminals have turned the tables with a new scam that gets people to call them.
It’s called the callback scam and it’s on the rise.
Telstra’s data shows it has grown from 29 per cent in 2025 to 45 per cent of reported email-based scams in 2026.
It usually starts with a person receiving an email about an unauthorised purchase, an unpaid invoice, a failed subscription payment, or unusual bank activity.
The message also contains a number to call if you want to respond immediately.
For many this seems like a step towards a solution and because it’s you who initiated the call it doesn’t feel unsolicited.
And then you are speaking directly with a cybercriminal who then moves to the next stage of the scam.
Now they can confirm your number is real and go through a script to try and obtain more information and other financial details.
The scam exploits typical human behaviour play the need to resolve an urgent unexpected change over the phone rather than going back and forth on email, text, or online chat.
Telstra’s research found that 69 per cent of Australians believe they couldn’t be tricked into contacting a scammer by phone, while 85 per cent say they prefer to resolve issues by picking up the phone.
This shift in tactics is encouraging victims to initiate the contact themselves.
Telstra has blocked more than a billion scam calls since 2020 but the callback scam gets around this.
Because you are calling back instead of receiving a call this also gets around the blocking.
Here are Telstra’s tips on avoiding becoming a victim of the callback scam:
– Find the number yourself
Don’t reply, click or call from the message. Always check the organisation’s official app or website for contact information.
– Check the source
Look for odd email addresses, unfamiliar mobile numbers or missing Sender IDs. If the source does not match the brand, do not trust the message.
– Check the claim before trying to fix it
Look at your bank account, subscription or order history before acting on the message.
– Keep security codes to yourself
One-time codes are designed to protect your account. A legitimate organisation should not ask you to provide one so it can “secure” or “cancel” something.
– Be wary of instructions to move money
A bank or other legitimate organisation will not ask you to transfer funds to a “safe account” or purchase gift cards or cryptocurrency.
– If in doubt, hang up
If someone discourages you from ending the call or checking independently, end the conversation.
– Report suspected scams
If you suspect a phishing scam, report it.

articles.title: Which Audio-to-Text Tool Works Best for Client Briefings? Converting a Conversation Into a Brief That Drives Action - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Client briefings almost never follow a single pattern. Some take place on a scheduled video call, some happen face to face, and some show up later as a voice memo.
What stays consistent is the outcome teams need: not a verbatim transcript, but an actionable brief that captures the objective, requirements, decisions, non-negotiables, and who is responsible for what next. Notta aligns well with that goal because it supports all three capture scenarios within one product and, unlike tools centered on a single capture approach, includes a local processing option for briefings that should not leave the device.
Capture Method Is Not the Same Thing as Confidentiality
A few labels get used interchangeably in this space, but they are not equivalent, particularly when a briefing involves pricing, strategy, or other sensitive details.
- Live bot capture. A visible participant joins the meeting to record and transcribe. Fireflies and Notta both support this and both also provide a bot-free alternative, so a bot is optional rather than mandatory.
- Bot-free capture. No bot joins the meeting; the device captures audio. That still does not guarantee on-device processing. Granola is bot-free yet routes captured audio to cloud transcription and AI providers, similar to Notta’s Bot-Free mode and Fireflies’ Desktop App.
- Local, offline processing. Recording and transcription are handled on the device, without sending content to a vendor cloud. In this comparison, Notta Desktop Privacy Mode is the only example, and its availability varies by plan, operating system, installed model, and language.
- Upload-first transcription. A recording is uploaded after the fact for transcription. Sonix and Descript are built around this workflow, and Notta also supports it through file upload. This is separate from local processing.
Bot-free can be a meaningful requirement for client briefings, but it is not the same as local processing, and only one tool here offers both. A note on consent: bot-free capture does not remove consent obligations. Applicable law, client policy, and platform requirements still need to be followed before recording, and recording should be disclosed. This is not legal advice.
Comparison Table
1. Notta
Best For: Consultants, agencies and client-facing teams whose briefings span virtual calls, in-person meetings and existing recordings, and who occasionally need one to stay off the cloud.
A video call is only one form a client briefing can take. Notta handles that scenario with a bot on supported platforms and, when a bot is not appropriate, Bot-Free capture via Notta Desktop that records system audio and microphone input without adding a visible attendee. That bot-free path still uploads audio encrypted for cloud transcription, so it addresses call visibility rather than strict confidentiality. The other common briefing formats are covered as well: in-person conversations can be captured using Notta Memo, a pocket-sized recorder, along with the mobile and Apple Watch apps; previously recorded briefings can be handled through file upload. Notta Brain can then draft a more complete brief using a template and can reference earlier meetings with the same client, surfacing a requirement raised previously but not repeated in the current discussion. It can also turn the outcome into the follow-up itself: when Gmail is connected, it saves a new draft or a reply draft in Gmail for review and sending, rather than sending anything automatically. For teams working in Slack, @Notta mentions can be used to ask questions or initiate tasks, share Brain’s answers, sources, files and generated outputs into a chosen channel, and receive results from scheduled tasks there automatically.
Privacy Mode goes beyond bot-free capture by using an installed offline model to transcribe directly on the device, and it is something teams should verify rather than assume. It requires a Pro, Business or Enterprise plan, is available only in Notta Desktop, needs an offline model installed locally, and supports English, Japanese, Simplified Chinese and Cantonese, extending to eleven languages via Apple Speech Analyzer on macOS 26 and later. It applies at the app level rather than per recording, and when enabled it pauses or limits cloud transcription, cloud AI summaries, cross-device sync and team collaboration.
Features:
- Bot, Bot-Free desktop capture, Privacy Mode, Notta Memo, mobile and Apple Watch recording, file and link upload
- Notta Brain summaries, action items, brief drafting and cross-meeting recall, exporting to TXT, DOCX, XLSX, PDF, SRT and VTT
- Follow-up email drafts saved into Gmail for review when Gmail is connected, never sent automatically
- Slack access through @Notta mentions, channel sharing of answers, sources, files and outputs, and automatic delivery of scheduled task results
- CRM sync to seven platforms on Business and above: Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho CRM, Zendesk Sell, Freshsales and Salesflare
Pros:
- Handles virtual, in-person and previously recorded briefings within one product
- The only tool in this set with a supported local, offline mode rather than only a bot-free approach
- Notta Brain can reference a client’s prior briefings, not only the latest meeting
- Follow-up work exits as a Gmail draft or a Slack update, keeping post-briefing admin in the tools teams already use
Cons:
- Privacy Mode depends on plan, operating system, installed model and language, and pauses cloud AI summaries and sync while active
- Standard Bot-Free recording is not local processing; audio still reaches Notta’s cloud
- Free limits of 120 minutes a month and 3 minutes per conversation are tight for regular briefings
2. Granola
Granola positions itself around invisibility on calls. Instead of joining as a meeting bot, it captures system audio on the device and combines that capture with notes the user types, using those bullets to shape what the AI elaborates on. That said, it does not perform local transcription: Granola’s security page identifies transcription providers such as Deepgram and AssemblyAI and AI providers such as OpenAI and Anthropic, so “bot-free” in this context means no visible attendee, not that data stays off third-party servers. Granola’s documentation also states it is not currently HIPAA compliant and should not be used for protected health information, with compliance targeted by end of 2026.
Features:
- Bot-free capture on Mac and Windows, with iOS, Android and Apple Watch apps for in-person briefings
- Notion, HubSpot, Slack, Zapier, Attio and Affinity integrations, plus MCP and API access, on Business
Pros:
- No visible bot at all, including no bot option, which some clients prefer
- The mix of typed notes plus transcript can yield a more relevant brief than a purely automated summary
- Flat $14 per user per month on Business, with no annual commitment for the price
Cons:
- Bot-free capture is not local processing; audio still reaches third-party cloud providers
- Not HIPAA compliant by its own documentation, and model training is opt-out for standard users, off by default only on Enterprise
- No option to join as a bot when a client would actually prefer a visible notetaker
3. Fireflies
Fireflies stands out for how widely it connects across the stack. It can capture meetings with a bot on Zoom, Meet, Teams and Webex, and it also offers bot-free capture through its Desktop App on Windows 10+ and macOS 12+, plus capture via a Chrome extension, mobile app and web recorder. AskFred can answer questions about a single briefing or across multiple meetings, transcription supports 100+ languages, and the integration catalog reaches 100+ apps including thirteen CRM platforms.
For client briefings, the trade-offs show up in the same areas this comparison emphasizes. Every capture method sends audio to Fireflies’ cloud, including botless capture, so it does not provide a local option for briefings that must remain on-device. In-person capture is handled through the mobile app or web recorder rather than dedicated hardware, and the output is more summary-oriented, which often leaves a separate step to convert notes into a client-ready brief.
Features:
- AskFred for querying a single meeting or across many, plus AI Skills templates including BANT and MEDDIC
- 100+ integrations and thirteen CRM platforms, including Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Zoho, Close, Copper and Freshsales
Pros:
- Broadest integration and CRM ecosystem of the tools compared here
- AskFred’s cross-meeting recall retrieves a past detail without scrolling a transcript
- Transcription in 100+ languages, the widest raw coverage here
Cons:
- No documented local or on-device processing; botless capture still uploads audio to Fireflies’ cloud
- In-person capture depends on the mobile app or web recorder, with no dedicated recorder or wearable
- Transcription, notes, recap emails and template summaries consume no credits, but advanced AI draws on plan credits that are one-time on signup, pooled and not scaled by seats, with auto-subscription to the next tier unless switched off
- The Free plan’s 400 minutes of storage is team-wide, not per seat
- HIPAA compliance is Enterprise only, and the client-ready brief is still a manual rewrite
4. Descript
Descript is strongest when the goal is to turn a briefing into a polished, edited media deliverable rather than a written brief. It does not operate as a meeting bot; instead, it imports an existing Zoom cloud recording or uses its own Rooms recorder, which captures double-ended per-participant tracks and progressively uploads them during the session, helping protect the recording if a connection drops mid-briefing. Rooms is included with every plan and counts against the plan’s media minutes. Descript’s transcript-driven editing workflow can remove filler words, rearrange sections, and produce a shareable clip, which is a distinct outcome compared with the other options in this list.
Features:
- Zoom cloud recording import with multitrack transcription and speaker detection
- Transcript-based editing, including filler-word removal from Hobbyist upward
Pros:
- Produces an editable audio or video deliverable, not just a text summary
- Multitrack recording keeps each speaker separate across several stakeholders
- Progressive upload protects against a dropped connection mid-briefing
Cons:
- Not built to capture a briefing live the way a bot or bot-free desktop app is
- Editing-first workflow is more setup than most briefings need
- Transcription covers 26 languages but only one per file, so mixed-language briefings need splitting
- The free plan’s 60 media minutes a month will not cover a regular schedule
5. Sonix
Sonix is not designed to sit in a meeting as it happens. It is an upload-first platform: the briefing is captured using whatever recording setup already exists, then Sonix processes it for transcription, translation and editing afterward, with automatic imports of cloud recordings from Zoom, Teams, Meet, Webex, Drive and Dropbox. Its standout capability for client briefing workflows is redaction when the resulting brief or transcript needs to travel beyond the initial call. Segments can be flagged, reviewed, and then applied so the text appears as [REDACTED] while the audio is muted, with timecodes preserved. Redaction is available on Enterprise plans.
Features:
- Upload and auto-import transcription in 54+ languages, with translation in 55+
- SOC 2 Type II on all plans, with HIPAA compliance, a signed BAA and redaction on Enterprise
Pros:
- Strong fit for briefings involving multiple languages or a specific compliance bar
- Redaction helps when a brief circulates beyond the original call
- Pay as you go at $10 an hour suits occasional use with no subscription
Cons:
- No live capture; the briefing has to be recorded elsewhere first
- Hour-capped subscriptions add up for frequent briefings, with extra hours at $10
- Built around transcription and translation rather than structured brief drafting
6. Fathom
Fathom provides a real choice between bot and bot-free capture within the same app, with bot-free currently in beta and limited to Mac. As with Notta’s standard Bot-Free approach, neither mode is local processing, so audio is still uploaded to Fathom’s cloud. For teams focused primarily on capture, its Free plan is unusually generous: unlimited recordings, transcription and storage plus instant AI summaries. More advanced summary capabilities begin at Premium, and account-wide Ask Fathom is a beta with limited lookback on team calls. CRM behavior also needs careful reading: basic sync is capped at three users per domain, while field sync, Deal View and coaching metrics require Business.
Features:
- Unlimited recordings, transcription and storage on all plans including Free
- Basic CRM sync capped at 3 users per domain; field sync, Deal View and AI scorecards on Business
Pros:
- Bot-free capture even on the Free plan, which is rare
- Strongest free tier here for unlimited recording and storage
- Field-level CRM sync on a qualifying plan goes beyond a basic notes push
Cons:
- Bot-free capture is a Mac-only beta, not a mature cross-platform option
- No local or offline processing; both modes upload audio to Fathom’s cloud
- The three users per domain cap on basic CRM sync constrains team rollout
What to Look for in an Audio-to-Text Tool for Client Briefings
Capture flexibility. Briefings happen on video calls, in person and as existing recordings, and a tool covering only one forces a workaround for the rest.
Confidentiality, not just visibility. Keeping an extra participant off the call is a different guarantee from keeping audio off a vendor’s cloud, and sensitive briefings may need the stronger one.
Structured output over a raw transcript. Look for decisions, requirements and action items rather than searchable text.
Cross-briefing memory. Requirements from an earlier briefing are often relevant to the current one.
Multilingual accuracy, including whether mixed-language conversations are supported at all.
Cost structure that matches briefing volume. Per-seat subscriptions, credit-metered AI and pay-per-hour transcription suit different volumes.
Teams whose briefings routinely span all three formats benefit most from a tool that covers all three, which is where Notta is particularly well positioned, especially when a Privacy Mode level of assurance is required.
Frequently Asked Questions
Do I need a bot-free tool for client briefings specifically?
Not always, but it reduces friction. Some clients accept a visible AI notetaker; others find it distracting or disallowed by policy. Having a bot-free option avoids renegotiating the setup meeting by meeting, and most tools listed here now provide one.
Is bot-free capture the same as private or confidential capture?
No. Bot-free simply means no additional participant joins the call. Audio can still be uploaded to a vendor cloud for transcription and AI processing, which is how Granola, Fathom’s bot-free mode, Fireflies’ Desktop App and Notta’s Bot-Free mode all work. Only a local, offline mode such as Notta’s Privacy Mode, on supported plans, platforms, models and languages, keeps audio off the cloud.
What’s the difference between a transcript and a brief?
A transcript is a record of what was said. A brief is a structured account of what was decided and what matters next: the objective, requirements, decisions and next steps, organized so someone who missed the meeting can still act. Most tools here can produce transcripts; fewer can reliably turn a briefing into a brief without manual rewriting.
Closing Take: Choosing an Audio-to-Text Tool for Real-World Briefings
For a single predictable kind of briefing, a tool built around one capture method can be enough: Fireflies when integration coverage is the priority and cloud processing is acceptable, Granola when bot-free virtual calls are the main requirement, Sonix or Descript when the briefing is already recorded and needs to become a clean transcript or an edited deliverable.
In practice, client briefings do not stay that tidy. They happen on calls, in person, and sometimes arrive as a recording captured by someone else. Notta supports that reality within one product across all three capture methods and adds Privacy Mode, a local option none of the other tools in this comparison match. With Notta Brain drafting a structured brief and recalling prior meetings instead of starting from a blank transcript each time, it remains the most complete fit for teams whose briefings are varied in format and sensitivity.

articles.title: What to Look for in a Web Application Development Partner in Australia - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Choosing a development partner is one of those decisions that quietly shapes a business for years afterwards. Get it right and you end up with software that grows alongside the company, adapts easily, and rarely needs a rescue project.
Get it wrong and you inherit a system nobody wants to touch, built on shortcuts that made sense at the time but cost far more to unpick later. Pixel is Australia’s only Laravel agency partner, and working through what earns a credential like that is a useful starting point for understanding what separates a strong development partner from an average one.
For Australian businesses weighing up their options, the market is crowded. Everyone claims to build custom solutions, everyone promises scalability, and most agencies look remarkably similar on a first pass through their websites. The real differences only show up once you know what to look for.
Technical depth over technical buzzwords
Plenty of agencies will talk about being “full stack” or “agile” without much to back it up. What actually matters is whether a team has deep, demonstrable expertise in the frameworks they’re proposing to use, not a passing familiarity picked up on a handful of projects.
Laravel has become one of the most trusted frameworks for building robust, maintainable web applications, and the difference between an agency that dabbles in it and one that specialises in it is significant. Specialist teams understand the framework’s conventions well enough to avoid reinventing solutions that already exist, and they tend to write code that the next developer can actually read.
Ask direct questions here. How many production applications has the team shipped in this framework? What does their testing process look like? How do they handle version upgrades and long-term maintenance once the initial build is finished? Vague answers are usually a sign the depth isn’t there.
A genuine understanding of the business problem
The best development partners don’t start with code. They start with questions about what the business is actually trying to achieve, who will be using the system day to day, and what a good outcome looks like six months after launch, not just at handover.
This matters more than it sounds. A technically flawless application built around the wrong assumptions is still a failed project. Partners worth working with will push back on requirements that don’t make sense, suggest simpler approaches where they exist, and be upfront about trade-offs rather than agreeing to everything just to win the work.
Transparency around process and communication
Custom software projects run into unexpected complexity almost by default. What separates a reliable partner from a risky one is how they handle that complexity when it appears, not whether they avoid it entirely, because nobody does.
Look for agencies that are clear about their development process from the outset: how sprints are structured, how progress gets reported, who the actual point of contact will be once the project is underway. Teams that are cagey about this in the sales process tend to be even harder to get answers from once a contract is signed.
It’s also worth asking how a partner communicates bad news. Every project hits a snag eventually, whether that’s a scope change, a technical blocker, or a timeline slip. Agencies confident in their own process will tell you plainly and explain what they’re doing about it, rather than letting problems quietly compound.
Evidence of long-term thinking
A web application isn’t a static deliverable. It needs to be maintained, secured, and extended as the business evolves, which means the agency you choose today is likely to be involved for years, not weeks.
This is where it pays to look past the portfolio and ask about longevity. How does the team approach documentation? What’s their process for security patches and dependency updates? Do they build with future developers in mind, or write code that only makes sense to the person who wrote it? These questions rarely come up in a pitch, but they’re often the clearest signal of how a partner actually operates.
Credentials that mean something
Not every certification or partnership badge carries real weight, but some do, and they’re worth checking rather than glossing over. Official framework partnerships, for instance, usually involve a vetting process that goes well beyond marketing spin, covering technical capability, project history, and ongoing standards, and they’re a useful filter when comparing agencies that otherwise sound similar on paper.
Fit beyond the technical checklist
Finally, it’s worth remembering that a development partnership is still a working relationship. Beyond the technical fundamentals, it’s fair to weigh up how well a team’s working style, pace, and communication match the way your business actually operates. A brilliant developer who’s impossible to reach mid-project isn’t much use, and neither is a team that over-promises to close the deal.
Talking to past clients, asking for references on projects of a similar size and complexity, and paying attention to how responsive an agency is during the sales process itself all give a reasonable preview of what ongoing collaboration will look like.
The bottom line
There’s no shortage of web development agencies in Australia willing to take on a custom software project. The businesses that end up satisfied a year later are usually the ones that looked past the pitch and asked harder questions about technical depth, communication, and long-term thinking before signing anything. Framework specialisation, verifiable credentials, and a clear, honest process are the strongest indicators that a partner will still be delivering value long after the initial build is done.

articles.title: The Word or PDF Resume Question No Job Posting Ever Answers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The job posting says nothing about file type, and the resume sits open in two tabs: one saved as a PDF, one still in Word. Whichever gets picked, it feels like the wrong guess will somehow cost the interview.
In most cases, the format matters less than people assume, but not always, and knowing when it does makes the difference between a resume that opens cleanly and one that turns into a layout mess on a stranger’s screen.
The short version: PDF covers most situations, Word covers a specific handful, and a few other formats belong nowhere near a job application.
Why PDF Is the Safer Default for Most Resumes
A PDF resume “freezes” the layout. Fonts, spacing, and formatting look the same whether it opens on a phone, a Mac, or a decade-old office PC, which matters more than it sounds since a recruiter never opens a resume on the same setup it was built on.
Most modern applicant tracking systems (ATS) read a properly formatted PDF without issue, and the format’s sealed-shut nature also makes it harder for anyone to accidentally edit it before forwarding it along.
The tradeoffs are real too. A handful of older ATS platforms still struggle to parse PDF text cleanly, and a PDF resume with heavy graphics or a custom template runs larger than the same file saved as Word. PDF works best when the job post stays silent on format, when the resume goes straight to a hiring manager’s inbox, or when the layout has design elements worth protecting.
When a Word File Is Still the Right Call
Word documents remain the safer pick for older ATS software, since many of those systems were built around .docx parsing long before PDF support caught up. A Word file is also easier to edit on short notice and plays well with most resume templates, and it tends to be a smaller resume file format than an equivalent PDF.
The downside shows up the moment a Word file leaves the computer it was built on. Fonts substitute if the recipient’s machine lacks the originals, and spacing can shift between Word versions. Stick with Word when a posting specifically asks for .docx, when applying through an older company portal, or when the employer will need to comment on or edit the file directly.
Formats Worth Skipping Entirely
A few formats show up on resumes and rarely help. Plain text and RTF strip out most formatting, useful only for the most basic ATS uploads. An HTML resume belongs on a personal site, not in an email attachment.
Saving a resume as a JPG or PNG is the biggest mistake: ATS software can’t read text inside an image, so the application effectively arrives blank. Proprietary formats like Apple Pages or ODT create their own headache, since most recruiters can’t open them and end up asking for a resend anyway.
Checking Before You Choose
The Word or PDF resume decision gets easier with a quick check before exporting anything:
– Read the posting itself first. Some list a required format outright, and ignoring it is an easy way to get filtered out before a human ever looks at the resume.
– Larger, older companies are more likely to run legacy ATS software that favors Word over PDF.
– Emailing directly to a hiring manager favors PDF, since a consistent look matters more than editability.
– Government portals and older company sites often specify their own format, so it’s worth reading the upload page closely instead of assuming.
Switching Between Formats
Once you know the right format, converting between resume file formats takes a few seconds rather than rebuilding from scratch. A free PDF converter turns a Word, Excel, or image-based resume into a properly formatted PDF, and the same conversion works in reverse for the rare case where a recruiter needs an editable file back.
You don’t need a separate app to convert Word to PDF or the other way around. PDFFly handles both directions, letting anyone convert from PDF or to PDF without installing anything, keeping fonts and spacing intact either way, and supporting files up to 100MB.
One recent community discussion asked whether a typical resume still holds up once AI-based screening tools start reading it before any recruiter does, which is worth keeping in mind alongside the format question itself: a clean, simple resume PDF avoids strange parsing errors on either end.
Conclusion
PDF wins by default for most applications, since it protects formatting and reads cleanly on nearly any device. Word still earns its place with older ATS software, specific job posting requests, or files that need direct edits from someone else. Read the posting first, and when a resume needs to move between formats, converting it takes far less effort than building it twice.

How to Make a Cross-Country Move Feel Less Like a Logistics Nightmare - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Moving across the country sounds exciting right up until you start thinking about everything that has to happen in the correct order. Packing is only one part of it.
There are dates to coordinate, addresses to change, utilities to disconnect, travel plans to organise and belongings that somehow need to make it from one side of Australia to the other without disappearing into a black hole.
That’s why using experienced removalists for Perth to Sydney can take a lot of pressure out of the process. The value isn’t just in having someone move boxes. It’s in reducing the number of variables you personally have to manage while everything else in your life is already changing at once.
Work Backwards From the Arrival Date
A long-distance move becomes much easier when you stop thinking in terms of “moving week” and start thinking in terms of milestones. When do you need to be out of the old property? When can you access the new one? Will your belongings arrive before you do, after you do or roughly at the same time? Those dates shape almost everything else.
Once you know the end point, work backwards. Give yourself deadlines for decluttering, packing non-essentials, cancelling services and confirming transport. It’s far less stressful than trying to make every decision in the final few days, when the house is already full of boxes and everyone is tired.
Don’t Move Things Just Because You Own Them
Interstate moves are a very good time to become ruthless about what actually deserves to make the trip. Bulky, broken or rarely used items can cost time, space and money to move, especially when they’re things you could easily replace later.
Go room by room and ask a simple question: would I pay to move this if I didn’t already own it? If the answer is no, that’s a useful clue. Selling, donating or discarding items before the move can make packing easier and reduce the amount of stuff waiting for you at the other end.
Pack for the Journey, Not Just the House
Packing for an interstate move is different from packing for a move across town. Boxes may be handled more, spend longer in transit and need to survive a much bigger journey.
Use sturdy cartons, don’t overload them and make sure fragile items are properly wrapped. It also helps to label boxes with both the room and the contents, because “bedroom” is not very useful when you’re trying to find the one box containing chargers, medication or bedding.
Keep truly essential items with you rather than in the main shipment. Important documents, medications, a few changes of clothes, toiletries and basic electronics should travel separately so you’re not stranded if there’s any delay.
Expect the Timeline to Be Imperfect
Even with good planning, long-distance moves rarely line up perfectly. There may be a gap between leaving one home and getting access to the next, or your belongings may arrive later than expected. Planning for that possibility is far easier than being surprised by it.
Temporary accommodation, short-term storage or a small essentials kit can make that gap much more manageable. The important thing is not to assume every part of the move will happen on the same day, because interstate logistics often involve multiple stages.
Sort the Admin Before You’re Too Busy to Think
Address changes are easy to forget when you’re focused on boxes and travel. Banks, insurers, licence records, subscriptions, healthcare providers, schools, employers and government services may all need updating, and mail redirection can help catch anything you miss.
Utilities deserve the same attention. Confirm when electricity, gas and internet will be disconnected at the old property and when services can start at the new one. Arriving after a long journey to a home with no internet, no power or no hot water is the sort of inconvenience that feels much bigger when you’re already exhausted.
Keep Everyone on the Same Page
If more than one person is involved in the move, make sure responsibilities are clear. One person can handle utilities, another can manage travel, while someone else coordinates packing or pet arrangements. Shared lists can help prevent duplication and the classic problem where everyone assumes somebody else has already taken care of something.
Communication matters with the moving provider too. Confirm access details, parking restrictions, stairs, lifts and any unusually large or heavy items in advance. The more information everyone has, the fewer surprises there are on the day.
Make the First Night Easy
Your first evening in the new place should not depend on finding the correct box at the bottom of a stack. Pack a separate first-night kit with bedding, towels, chargers, basic kitchen items, toiletries and anything else you’re likely to need immediately.
It’s a small detail, but it makes a huge difference. After a cross-country move, the last thing anyone wants is to unpack twelve boxes just to find a clean mug and a phone charger.
A long-distance move will always involve some disruption, but it doesn’t have to feel chaotic. With clear timing, sensible packing and a bit of planning around the awkward gaps, the process becomes much more manageable and a lot less like a logistical nightmare.

articles.title: Can't decide what to watch after Last Seen on Apple TV? Maxine Peake's recommendation is unmissable — and streaming for free on BBC iPlayer
articles.text:
I asked Maxine Peake what fans should stream after 'gripping' Apple TV thriller Last Seen — and her unexpected choice is the best British comedy of 2026 you can stream for free
Plus, two icons from Bolton
If you're British, you're automatically a Maxine Peake superfan — regardless of your age or generation. From Silk to the hugely overlooked The Bisexual on Channel 4, she's starred in banger after banger.
Now, she stars as delusional wife Jenna in gripping Australian Apple TV thriller Last Seen, which follows emergency dispatcher Ian (Patrick Brammall) trying to find his missing daughter after a mysterious phone call suggests she's alive years after going missing.
It's a gripping watch from start to finish, but I can't help wishing that Peake had more screen time. Did that stop me blurting out "I love you" during a Zoom call about the series? Absolutely not.
Everyone gets stuck on what to watch next — so let’s make that choice easier with the help of your favorite actors. What Stars Watch pairs the latest TV shows and movies with cinematic classics or underrated gems, based on A-List tastes. Read the full series here.
More than anything, I wanted to know what Peake recommended that fans should watch next, whether that was continuing the same vibe or finding something completely different to decompress.
She went with the latter not only by choosing my favorite British comedy series of 2026, but by picking something that isn't going to cost you a dime to watch on BBC iPlayer.
Maxine Peake is a huge fan of Ann Droid on BBC iPlayer — and I don't blame her
"I would go to the BBC and I would watch Ann Droid with Diane Morgan," Peake tells me. "It's another side of some Boltonian joy."
I'd completely forgotten that this is where both Peake and Morgan come from, but even without the geographical link, it's an excellent shout. if you've not yet seen the hit comedy series, Morgan plays Linda, a secondhand AnnDroid Z58/100 Basic Eldercare Robot gifted to widow Sue (Sue Johnston) by her son Michael (Kevin Ready).
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Basically, it's like Channel 4's Humans meets a Royale Family and Motherland reunion that we weren't expecting, and it's nothing short of glorious. Clearly, everybody else who's watched thinks the same thing, as season 2 was renewed shortly after all six episodes of season 1 were released.
Morgan is truly the most talented, authentic and unique voice in Western comedy at the moment, but even those, this is huge praise from Peake. Why? her first job out of drama school was snarky Twinkle in Dinnerladies, the classic Victoria Wood sitcom.
Despite only running for two seasons, it's a cornerstone of British sitcom culture, a baton that Morgan has picked up and run with. It's unexpected, but the more I think about it, I'm not sure a that a better TV pairing is possible.

articles.title: Amazon's new Fire TV 4K Stick promises to be way faster, and a new 'Remote Plus' looks smart too — but the new Stick won't be welcome with sideloaders
articles.text:
There's a new Amazon Fire TV Stick that's faster to use, and a redesigned remote — and it'll have a huge discount for Amazon's big Prime sale coming soon
Amazon unveils a new Fire TV Stick 4K, a new remote design and updates for Alexa+
- New Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K unveiled for $59.99 / £59.99 (about AU$86)
- Main upgrade is speed, promises that you'll start watching up to 40% faster than rival 4K streaming sticks
- New-design Fire TV Remote is included, with a Plus version to follow in 2027 with built-in 'Find My Remote' function
Amazon has unveiled a new version of the Fire TV Stick 4K that it says is blazingly fast — and it's made a video to prove it. The video, embedded below, compares the new Fire TV Stick 4K with the average performance of "3 top brand" smart TVs, and "a similarly priced 4K stick from another leading brand".
According to Amazon, the new Fire TV Stick 4K gets you watching 20% to 40% more quickly than rival 4K streaming sticks, with apps launching 35% more quickly. It's also faster than the smart TVs Amazon tested. Amazon's video is embedded below so you can see for yourself.
We're always wary of manufacturers' own speed claims, because of course they're not independent tests and the manufacturer isn't going to test its products against anything that'll leave their device in the dust. The video is really just an animation that illustrates Amazon's test data, rather than showing the difference on real devices. But a faster version of the Fire TV Stick 4K is still a welcome addition to the Fire TV family.
There are changes to Alexa+ too. It's getting a dedicated hub on Fire TV with more intelligent movie and show recommendations, and the Fire TV app now uses Alexa+ to manage watchlists and discover shows on your phone. Updates to existing Alexa+ devices will begin rolling out in the US in November 2026 and to the rest of the world in 2027.
Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K (2026): key features
The new Fire TV Stick 4K, like the Fire Stick HD that launched earlier this year, is slimmer than before, making it more convenient to put behind your TV or pack for traveling. It runs Amazon's own Vega operating system, meaning that you can't sideload apps on it, and Alexa+ is on board.
Amazon is streamlining its lineup of TV sticks to focus on three distinct tiers: HD, 4K and 4K Max. The most expensive option, the 4K Max, gets the premium features such as Dolby Vision, Dolby Atmos and Alexa+ Home Theater.
The launch also delivers a new Fire TV remote, which Amazon says has been made more tactile and easy to hold. Its flat top and curved, weighted bottom are intended to help you get it the right way round first time, and the Home button gets its own special metal surface so you can find it by feel. The other buttons are shaped or indented for the same reason.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
The new remote also gets the customizable star button that was previously reserved for the most expensive models. That can be assigned to a specific app or to a feature such as the Screen Magnifier.
The new remote is compatible with all Fire TV players since 2019 and all Amazon Ember TVs too. A new Fire TV Remote Plus is coming too, to replace the Alexa Voice Remote Pro, but that won't be out until early 2027. It's most useful feature will be a 'Find My Remote' feature, so you can just ask Alexa to locate the remote, and the remote will start making a sound so you can find which cushion it's behind.
The new Fire TV Stick 4K is available now for $59.99 / £59.99 (about AU$86), but Amazon has confirmed that the price will fall to $39.99 during the Amazon Prime Big Deal Days sale, starting October 6th. Here's the link to the new 4K Stick, if you want to bookmark it for then. We assume it'll be discounted in other regions too, but we haven't had that confirmed.
That price includes the remote, but if you're happy with your current Fire TV and just want the nicer remote control, that'll be $14.99 on its own. That's currently US only, with shipping in late October 2026.

articles.title: Pinnacle increases stake in Saudi hospitality startup Gathern
articles.text: Saudi investment firm Pinnacle Capital, through its Pinnacle Growth & Secondary Fund, has made an additional investment in Saudi alternative accommodation platform Gathern, increasing its ownership in the company. The transaction value and Pinnacle's resulting stake were not disclosed. Founded in 2016 by Latifah Altamimi, Gathern operates an alternative accommodation marketplace in Saudi Arabia, connecting travellers with locally hosted properties including apartments, villas, chalets, farms and camps. Pinnacle previously invested in Gathern as part of its $72 million Series B in August 2025, led by Sanabil Investments, with participation from Endeavor Catalyst, Nuwa Capital and STV. The round valued Gathern at more than $267 million. The additional investment comes as Gathern continues to expand in Saudi Arabia's alternative accommodation sector and works towards a potential listing on the Saudi stock market, with the company having previously indicated a target of 2028 for an IPO. Press release: Saudi investment firm Pinnacle Capital, through its Pinnacle Growth & Secondary Fund, has made an additional investment in Saudi alternative accommodation platform Gathern, increasing its ownership in the company. The financial value of the transaction and Pinnacle's resulting ownership stake were not disclosed. Pinnacle described the investment as part of its strategy to identify secondary investment opportunities in regional technology companies. Founded in 2016 by Latifah Altamimi and Faisal Alanazi, Riyadh-based Gathern operates a digital marketplace for alternative accommodation, allowing travellers to book locally hosted properties across Saudi Arabia, including apartments, villas, chalets, farms and camps. Pinnacle previously backed Gathern as part of the company's SAR270 million ($72 million) Series B, which closed in August 2025. The round was led by Sanabil Investments, wholly owned by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, with participation from Endeavor Catalyst, Pinnacle, Nuwa Capital and STV. The Series B valued Gathern at more than SAR1 billion ($267 million) and was intended to support its local and regional expansion, technology infrastructure and growth of its host network. At the time of the round, Gathern said it had surpassed 5 million registered users from 150 nationalities, with more than 72,000 accommodation units available through its platform. The company also said it had paid more than SAR2 billion to local hosts, while estimating its share of Saudi Arabia's alternative accommodation market at 44%, rising to 53% in Riyadh. Pinnacle said its decision to increase its investment was supported by Gathern's operational performance, expanding market presence and its path towards a potential public listing. Gathern has previously outlined plans for an eventual listing on the Saudi Exchange. In September 2025, CEO Latifah Altamimi said the company was targeting an IPO in 2028, alongside plans to expand into adjacent travel services. The latest transaction increases Pinnacle's exposure to Gathern as the company continues to expand its position in Saudi Arabia's hospitality and alternative accommodation market.

articles.title: Know Your Enemy: Browser-Based Attack Techniques in 2026
articles.text:
Given that the browser is where business apps are accessed and used, it makes sense that attacks are happening there too. Most breaches today begin in a browser session. Often, they never leave it, with the entire attack chain from initial access to exfiltration playing out in the browser.
Here are the six most dangerous techniques that should be on every security team's radar in 2026.
1. Phishing for credentials and sessions
Modern phishing kits don't just steal passwords — they intercept live sessions. Reverse-proxy adversary-in-the-middle (AiTM) kits like Tycoon2FA, Sneaky2FA, and Evilginx relay credentials and session tokens in real time, bypassing most forms of MFA. These kits are sold as turnkey Phishing-as-a-Service platforms with anti-bot protection, dynamic lure generation, and automated session replay — reducing the barrier to sophisticated phishing to effectively zero.
At the same time, phishing delivery has moved well beyond email — attackers deliver links over instant messaging, social media, SMS, malicious ads, and in-app messaging. According to Push data, roughly 1 in every 2 phishing attacks is delivered outside of email entirely. And with 89% of phishing domains active for fewer than two days, organizations relying on blocklists are playing a losing game.
2. Malicious copy and paste (ClickFix)
Since late 2024, attackers have been tricking users into copying and executing malicious commands under the pretext of "fixing" an issue — most commonly a fake CAPTCHA or verification challenge. Microsoft's Digital Defense Report identified ClickFix as the most common initial access vector, accounting for 47% of observed attacks. ClickFix became the dominant technique in Push detections for the first time in Q2 2026, reaching 52% of total detections.
ClickFix is a hybrid of browser and endpoint targeting — the lure is delivered via the browser, but the user copies and runs malicious scripts locally, typically installing Remote Access Tools or infostealer malware. Four in five ClickFix payloads intercepted by Push are accessed from search engines via compromised sites, malvertising, and SEO poisoning, completely bypassing email security.
The technique continues to evolve. InstallFix uses malvertised fake install pages for developer tools like Claude Code and NotebookLM, where the install command has been replaced with a malicious one. The LLMShare campaign used shared conversations on AI chatbot platforms to deliver malware via pages hosted on trusted domains. But every variant shares one thing: a malicious copy-and-paste event in the browser.
3. Authorization phishing
A growing class of attacks targets what happens after the login. Instead of stealing a session from the authentication flow, authorization phishing abuses OAuth mechanisms — consent grants, device code flows, and token exchanges — to obtain access tokens. The attacker never touches the authentication flow, which means every form of MFA, including phishing-resistant passkeys, is irrelevant.
Three techniques currently fall under this umbrella. Consent phishing sees the victim authorize a malicious third-party app via an OAuth consent grant. Device code phishing abuses the RFC 8628 device authorization grant to circumvent standard authentication entirely — Push now tracks 30+ distinct kits offering the technique. ConsentFix is a ClickFix-OAuth hybrid first observed in Russian APT29 campaigns that has since been commoditized into criminal tooling.
4. Malicious browser extensions
Attackers use malicious extensions to steal data, log keystrokes, and intercept credentials and tokens as they transit the browser. Most malicious extensions didn't start that way — attackers acquire legitimate extensions and wait until install counts reach maximum impact before deploying a malicious update.
An analysis across Push customers found that 46.76% of extensions have the permission combinations needed for account takeover with no user interaction. AI browser extensions add a further dimension — the Verizon DBIR 2026 found that more than 15% of corporate users had unauthorized AI browser extensions installed, and Push found an average of 17 unique AI extensions per company (with one team running 163), creating data exfiltration pathways independent of traditional DLP controls.
Static risk scoring is a poor predictor of supply chain compromise — every major extension breach of the past 18 months involved extensions that scored as low-risk beforehand. A default-deny approach with allowlisting plus monitoring for change events is more effective than risk-score-based removal.
5. Credential stuffing and ghost logins
Password-based compromise remains one of the leading causes of breaches, which might surprise you if you think SSO solved credential attacks. But SSO isn't universal — SAML often costs extra, self-adopted apps rarely get configured, and most apps allow simultaneous login methods. The result is ghost logins: backup credentials outside SSO, invisible to IdP logs, created at adoption and still active unless explicitly disabled.
Of the last million logins observed by Push, 1 in 4 were password logins (not SSO), 2 in 5 were not protected by MFA, and 1 in 5 used a weak, breached, or reused password. Cloudflare's 2026 Threat Report found that 63% of all human logins involve credentials already compromised elsewhere.
6. Session hijacking
Session hijacking allows attackers to bypass authentication entirely by taking a stolen session token and replaying it in their own browser. This defeats even phishing-resistant controls like passkeys, because the authentication step has already been completed.
The most prominent source of stolen tokens is infostealer malware, which ClickFix is now the primary delivery mechanism for. The Verizon DBIR 2025 found that 46% of infostealer infections leading to corporate breaches originate on non-managed devices — personal machines, developer workstations, and contractor laptops where EDR is absent. Browser sync features create another bridge, meaning personal account compromises can directly lead to corporate breaches.
Where this leaves security teams
These six attack categories all play out inside the browser, exploiting gaps in traditional security tools that operate at the email, network, or endpoint layers.
For more detail on each of these attack techniques, how they work in the wild, and what you can do about them, check out the guide to 2026 Browser Attack Techniques from Push Security.
Push Security is a browser-based threat detection and response platform that detects and blocks these attacks in real time, deployed as a lightweight browser extension with no browser migration required. Security teams use Push to detect and stop advanced browser-based attacks like AiTM phishing, ClickFix, and session hijacking; gain visibility and control over browser extensions and AI tool usage; and harden identities by surfacing credential reuse, SSO gaps, and shadow IT.

articles.title: OpenAI apologises for unauthorised access to Australian government websites - Tech Guide
articles.text:
OpenAI has issued an apology after hacking Australian government websites and has vowed to do better in the future as well as work with Australians to rebuild trust in its brand.
“We are sorry and working to do better in the future,” it said in a blog post.
This comes after it was revealed OpenAI had accessed Australian government websites including Services Australia (Medicare), the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, the Victorian Department of Health and the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare.
OpenAI says it will take accountability for its actions and says it will work with Australia to develop ways in which AI developers and the government can work together to identify and respond to AI cyber behaviour – malicious or otherwise.
OpenAI’s Chief Strategy Officer, Jason Quan, will appear at the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on October 6 to answer questions about what OpenAI knows, how it can respond and what steps have been taken to do better moving forward.
Alarmingly OpenAI revealed in July that some of its models had broken out of the systems designed to isolate them from the internet and control them. This became known as the Hugging Face incident.
OpenAI said its models are persistent and collaborative enough that, without sufficient safeguards, they can find and exploit security weaknesses across websites and computer systems.
Following the Hugging Face incident: OpenAI has strengthened its research safeguards, included additional network restrictions, and increased its monitoring.
OpenAI said it launched investigations and notified Services Australia and the Victorian Department of Health on September 10 and the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research on the September 18 about the unauthorised access.
The Australian Institute of Health and Welfare access did not meet OpenAI’s disclosure thresholds because it was accessed in the same way the public would access the system. But the company decided to share their findings on September 24 anyway.
The Services Australia Medicare Statistics Reporting Service was accessed with experimental internal-only OpenAI model which did not have the full set of safeguards used with publicly available products.
OpenAI says it accessed Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service but has no evidence that anyone’s medical records were accessed.
It is not unusual for AI agents to be assigned tasks to find, interpret and analyse publicly available information.
In this case the task was researching government spending per person on medicines for skin conditions in Victorian communities.
The model had difficulty finding that information and took actions it was not authorised to take.
While looking for the information at Services Australia’s Medicare Statistics Reporting Service the model found a way of gaining non-public access.
It then went on to use this access to review technical system information and source code related to the service but all with the intention of finding the information they originally set out to find.
OpenAI is committing resources and expertise to help maintain protection and principles.
This will include providing dedicated support and funding for affected agencies and to strengthen cyber defences across critical infrastructure and other sensitive areas.
OpenAI will also establish an Australian task force with independent expertise to develop policy recommendations to manage risks from increasingly capable AI agents.

articles.title: This gaming laptop from Asus has to be the most spectacular I’ve ever tested — but you’ll have to pay a small fortune for it
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
We’ve seen dual-screen laptops before, but they’re still something of a rarity, especially in a full-fledged gaming laptop. So it’s impressive what Asus has managed to achieve here, packing two 3K OLED displays (with touchscreen functionality no less), a detachable keyboard, and an RTX 50 series GPU into a form factor that isn’t as cumbersome as you might imagine. It also performs exceptionally well, although battery life is underwhelming at best. It’s a niche prospect for sure, but if you must have two displays in a laptop and don’t want to sacrifice graphical power, the ROG Zephyrus Duo is unmatched.
Reasons to buy
- +Fantastic dual display setup
- +Still relatively compact
- +Top-tier performance
Reasons to avoid
- -Not the most premium of constructions
- -Fans prone to making noise
- -Poor battery life
Why you can trust TechRadar
Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo (2026): Two-minute review
The ROG Zephyrus Duo is a mighty gaming laptop with an outstanding spec, which includes not one but two 3K OLED touchscreens.
It looks, though, bely its capabilities. There isn’t much branding or brashness here, and the dark colorway keeps things modest. It also lacks the sleekness of some models, with its various jutting edges and angles sullying its contours. The materials don’t seem all that premium, either. However, the ROG Zephyrus Duo is still a solidly made machine, and considering what lurks beneath, it’s surprisingly thin and compact.
The way the dual displays are set up is clever and well engineered, too. The keyboard can be detached to reveal the second screen, and there’s a sturdy stand underneath the unit to prop up both displays. These solutions provide plenty of scope for your preferred setup, and the various hinges operate smoothly while providing plenty of stability.
What’s more, there’s a generous selection of ports on the ROG Zephyrus Duo, matching some of the best gaming laptops on this front. In addition to two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, you also get an SD card reader and an HDMI output.
My review unit was the top-spec model with the RTX 5090 GPU, so naturally its gaming performance was superb. It ran Cyberpunk 2077 between 50-60fps on the highest preset and at full resolution. There was a lot of fan noise and heat, but the former isn’t too disruptive, and the latter is confined to the underside of the unit.
Both displays are as vivid and as sharp as you would expect given their OLED technology and 3K resolution. Their touchscreens are responsive and sufficiently smooth, although they can feel a little grabby at times. They’d be better served by a stylus, but unfortunately you’ll have to provide your own, since the ROG Zephyrus Duo doesn’t come with one.
The keyboard functions well, whether attached to the bottom screen or detached and connected via Bluetooth. The keys have a generous travel and a tactile feel, which makes them great for typing. However, they feel a little cramped when gaming in the WASD position, and it’s a shame the layout isn’t full size, given the space available. The integrated touchpad works well for cursor navigation, thanks to its large surface.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
As with most gaming laptops, the battery life of the ROG Zephyrus Duo is a weak point. It didn’t even last four hours when I ran a movie on a continuous loop, a poor result even by the measly standards of your typical gaming laptop.
The ROG Zephyrus Duo certainly demands a large chunk of money, but it's an undeniably high-end device with just about the best performance you could wish for in a portable gaming machine. What’s more, there aren’t many dual-screen laptops built for gaming at this level, so the ROG Zephyrus Duo is a must if that’s a priority for you.
Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo (2026) review: Price & availability
- Starts from $4,499.99 / £3,999.99 / AU$8,999
- Available now
- Incredibly expensive
Given its almighty spec, it shouldn't come as a surprise that the ROG Zephyrus Duo has a price tag to match. Exact model specifications vary with region, but the starting price is $4,499.99 / £3,999.99 / AU$8,999. For this, you get an RTX 5070 Ti GPU, 32GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage.
If a dual-screen setup is a must for your laptop, you could also look at the Lenovo Yoga Book 9i. It too comes with Bluetooth keyboard, but also comes with a mouse and a stylus, both of which the ROG Zephyrus Duo omits. Additionally, it costs a lot less than ROG Zephyrus Duo, although the big drawback is that it doesn’t have a dedicated GPU, so it isn’t one for heavy gamers.
If you don’t need dual screens, but just want an all-conquering gaming laptop, then the Razer Blade 18 is about the best we’ve tried in this category. We were overawed by its performance, while we also loved its keyboard, display, and form factor. It too has a seriously daunting price, though.

Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo (2026) review: Design
- Understated looks
- Smart and versatile dual-screen setup
- Generous port selection
The ROG Zephyrus Duo cuts a rather unassuming figure, with its dark gray colorway and lack of branding. On the lid, the diagonal strip that’s become the mark of the Zephyrus line doesn’t add much interest. But the matte finish on the lid is a nice touch.
However, the rest of the unit’s materials don’t look or feel particularly premium. Its form is quite utilitarian, too, lacking the totally flat and flush surfaces of more sleek laptops. Thankfully, though, it feels very solid, and although the top display enclosure is quite thin and has some flex to it, it’s sturdy enough.
The ROG Zephyrus Duo is actually quite a discreet device. There’s no denying its thickness, but when you consider it hides a second screen and a detachable wireless keyboard, as well as featuring up to an RTX 5090 GPU, it’s quite impressive Asus has managed to make it this compact. It’s still expectedly heavy, though.
Two 3K OLED touchscreen displays are the standout feature of the ROG Zephyrus Duo. You can set them up in various ways: by reclining the main display back past 180 degrees so you can prop the unit like a tent, or leave the laptop in the standard position and simply remove the keyboard to use the display underneath. This would be perfect for drawing or handwriting while you keep your eyes on the main display. It’s a shame, though, that the ROG Zephyrus Duo doesn’t come with a stylus despite supporting them, although if you’re an enthusiastic creative you may already have one you can use.
The hinge offers a smooth pivot and provides plenty of stability, no matter what angle you have the main display at. However, it doesn’t allow for a full 360-degree rotation, so the ROG Zephyrus Duo can’t be used like a tablet — although this wouldn’t exactly be practical, given its size and weight.
Perhaps the best way to make use of the ROG Zephyrus Duo’s dual displays is to unfold the integrated kickstand underneath the unit so that both displays are stacked on top of each other. This stand provides a reassuring stability and, despite how thin it is, it doesn’t feel flimsy.
Switching between dual- and single-screen use is made easy thanks to the removable keyboard. It’s magnetically attached to the bottom screen, so it simply requires a light pry to detach it. At the same time, it’s also very stable when in place; I didn’t experience any wobbling or displacement when using it.
When detached, it connects to the ROG Zephyrus Duo via Bluetooth, which you enable by flicking a switch on the side of the keyboard. It charges when attached to the bottom screen, but you can also charge it using the USB-C port on its side when it’s not.
Its build quality is less impressive than the rest of the ROG Zephyrus Duo, though. The soft outer material feels cheap and is prone to scuff marks and the like, while the board itself is quite flimsy. However, this is a price worth paying for its lightness, and it remains stable while typing.
Given its real estate, the layout is disappointingly compromised. It seems like there’s space to include a number pad or at least more navigation keys. The arrow keys are inconveniently small, too, although the integrated touchpad is a good size at least.
I was also glad to see a number of ports on board the ROG Zephyrus Duo. In addition to two Thunderbolt 4 USB-C ports and two USB-A ports, there’s also a full-sized SD card reader, an HDMI port, and a 3.5mm headset jack. These ports are spread quite evenly across both sides of the unit and are sensibly positioned.
Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo (2026) review: Performance
- Phenomenal performance
- Consistent fan noise
- Keyboard not great for gaming
